notes.front: What is a code scanning alert?
notes.back: What GitHub displays in a repository when code scanning finds a potential vulnerability or error in the code.
notes.explanation: An alert is not permanent: once the code that triggered it is fixed, GitHub closes it.
notes.example: Like a snag list entry on a building site: it names the fault and where it is, and it is ticked off once the fault is repaired.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning”
notes.evidence: If code scanning finds a potential vulnerability or error in your code, GitHub displays an alert in the repository. After you fix the code that triggered the alert, GitHub closes the alert.

notes.front: What does the Affected branches section of a code scanning alert page show?
notes.back: The alert’s status on branches other than the default branch.
notes.explanation: The status and details at the top of the alert page describe the default branch only, so other branches need their own place.
notes.example: Like a parcel tracker whose headline shows the main depot, with a side panel listing the parcel’s status at each other depot.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: The status and details on the alert page only reflect the state of the alert on the default branch of the repository, even if the alert exists in other branches. You can see the status of the alert on non-default branches in the Affected branches section on the right-hand side of the alert page.

notes.front: What is data-flow analysis in code scanning?
notes.back: CodeQL analysis that follows how data moves through code to find issues such as insecure data use or leaked sensitive information.
notes.explanation: It is available when code scanning is configured with CodeQL, and it also catches dangerous arguments passed to functions.
notes.example: Like tracing a leak from the tap where water enters the pipes to the ceiling where it finally drips.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: If you configure code scanning using CodeQL, you can also find data-flow problems in your code. Data-flow analysis finds potential security issues in code, such as: using data insecurely, passing dangerous arguments to functions, and leaking sensitive information.

notes.front: What does it mean when a code scanning alert has multiple analysis origins?
notes.back: More than one code scanning configuration reported it; the alert page shows its status for each analysis origin.
notes.explanation: Running code scanning with multiple configurations is what gives one alert several origins.
notes.example: Like one fault logged by two separate inspectors, each keeping their own record of whether it has been put right.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Integration with code scanning”, “About integration with code scanning”
notes.evidence: If you run code scanning using multiple configurations, an alert will sometimes have multiple analysis origins. If an alert has multiple analysis origins, you can view the status of the alert for each analysis origin on the alert page.

notes.front: What is the severity of a code scanning alert?
notes.back: A level, `Error`, `Warning` or `Note`, that every code scanning alert has.
notes.explanation: The level indicates how much risk the problem adds to your codebase.
notes.example: Like a spell checker’s red, amber and blue underlines: every mark gets one of the three.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert severity and security severity levels”
notes.evidence: The severity level for a code scanning alert indicates how much risk the problem adds to your codebase. * Severity. All code scanning alerts have a level of `Error`, `Warning`, or `Note`.

notes.front: What is the security severity of a code scanning alert?
notes.back: An extra level, `Critical`, `High`, `Medium` or `Low`, carried by each security alert found using CodeQL.
notes.explanation: When an alert has one, code scanning displays and uses it in preference to the plain severity.
notes.example: Like a triage colour added to a hospital patient who already has a general “urgent” or “routine” flag: the colour is what staff act on.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert severity and security severity levels”
notes.evidence: Each security alert found using CodeQL also has a security severity level of `Critical`, `High`, `Medium`, or `Low`. When an alert has a security severity level, code scanning displays and uses this level in preference to the `severity`.

notes.front: What is Copilot Autofix?
notes.back: A feature that turns a code scanning alert’s description and location into suggested code changes that may fix it.
notes.explanation: The word “may” matters: a suggestion is a proposal, not a guaranteed fix.
notes.example: Like a grammar checker offering a rewrite of a flagged sentence, which you can accept, edit or ignore.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “How autofix works”
notes.evidence: Autofix translates the description and location of a code scanning alert into code changes that may fix it.

notes.front: What is agentic autofix?
notes.back: Assigning a code scanning alert to Copilot, which starts a Copilot cloud agent session that generates and validates a fix, then opens a pull request.
notes.explanation: The agent explores the codebase beyond the affected file and iterates, for example re-running CodeQL, until it opens the pull request.
notes.example: Like handing a repair ticket to a technician who investigates, repairs and tests, then asks you to sign off the work.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Agentic autofix”
notes.evidence: Assign a code scanning alert to Copilot to have it resolve the alert for you. Assigning an alert starts an agent session: Copilot cloud agent calls tools to explore your codebase beyond the affected file, generates a fix, validates it (for example, by re-running CodeQL), and iterates until it opens a pull request with the changes.

notes.front: What is code scanning merge protection?
notes.back: Code scanning rules added to a ruleset (a named list of rules for branches and tags) that stop risky pull requests from merging.
notes.explanation: The rules block a merge when a required code scanning tool reports a problem or has not produced results.
notes.example: Like a venue door that stays shut until the security scanner has checked each guest.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Rulesets for code scanning merge protection”
notes.evidence: A ruleset is a named list of rules that control how people can interact with branches and tags in your repositories. You can add code scanning rules to rulesets to prevent pull requests from being merged when any of the following conditions are met

notes.front: Where does GitHub display the alerts from different code scanning analyses of one repository?
notes.back: Alongside each other in the repository’s security view.
notes.explanation: Code scanning can combine the default CodeQL analysis, a third-party analysis or several types of analysis on the same repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts from code scanning”
notes.evidence: You can configure code scanning to check the code in a repository using the default CodeQL analysis, a third-party analysis, or multiple types of analysis. When the analysis is complete, the resulting alerts are displayed alongside each other in the security view of the repository.

notes.front: Besides the line of code that triggered it, what are two properties a code scanning alert shows?
notes.back: Any two of: severity, security severity, the nature of the problem (among others).
notes.explanation: Each alert also names the tool that identified the problem.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: Each alert highlights a problem with the code and the name of the tool that identified it. You can see the line of code that triggered the alert, as well as properties of the alert, such as the alert severity, security severity, and the nature of the problem.

notes.front: Which branch’s state do the status and details on a code scanning alert page reflect?
notes.back: Only the default branch’s, even when the alert also exists on other branches.
notes.explanation: The status on other branches is shown separately, in the Affected branches section.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: The status and details on the alert page only reflect the state of the alert on the default branch of the repository, even if the alert exists in other branches.

notes.front: A code scanning alert does not exist on the default branch. What status does its alert page show?
notes.back: “In pull request” or “in branch”, coloured grey.
notes.explanation: The page normally reports default-branch state, and these grey labels mark an alert found only elsewhere.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: If an alert doesn't exist in the default branch, the status of the alert will display as "in pull request" or "in branch" and will be colored grey.

notes.front: When code scanning reports a data-flow alert, what does GitHub show you?
notes.back: How data moves through the code.
notes.explanation: Following the data identifies code that leaks sensitive information or could be an entry point for attacks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: When code scanning reports data-flow alerts, GitHub shows you how data moves through the code. Code scanning allows you to identify the areas of your code that leak sensitive information, and that could be the entry point for attacks by malicious users.

notes.front: What does Show paths display on a data-flow alert?
notes.back: Each step of the data flow as a numbered list, from the source to the sink.
notes.explanation: The source is where user-provided data enters the code; the sink is where it is used in a potentially unsafe operation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assessing code scanning alerts for your repository”, “Viewing the alerts for a repository”
notes.evidence: The path view shows each step in the data flow as a numbered list, from the point where user-provided data enters the code (the source) to the point where it's used in a potentially unsafe operation (the sink).

notes.front: How does code scanning report one vulnerability that can be reached through several code paths?
notes.back: As a single alert grouping the related paths, not one alert per path.
notes.explanation: Grouping lets you see the full scope of the vulnerability in one place.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: Code scanning groups these related paths under a single alert rather than creating separate alerts for each path, so you can see the full scope of the vulnerability in one place.

notes.front: How can a team track code scanning remediation work in its own workflow without leaving GitHub?
notes.back: By linking the alerts to GitHub issues.
notes.explanation: Linking sits alongside the other ways of following an alert, such as its affected branches and linked pull requests.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: To track remediation work in your team's workflow without leaving GitHub, you can link alerts to issues.

notes.front: What does each configuration of code scanning on a repository generate?
notes.back: Its own unique set of alerts.
notes.explanation: Configurations can use different tools and target different languages or areas of the code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts from multiple configurations”
notes.evidence: You can run multiple configurations of code analysis on a repository, using different tools and targeting different languages or areas of the code. Each configuration of code scanning generates a unique set of alerts.

notes.front: An alert shows different statuses from different configurations. What are the two ways to bring it up to date?
notes.back: Re-run each out-of-date configuration, or delete stale configurations from the branch.
notes.explanation: Deleting a stale configuration removes its outdated alerts from that branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts from multiple configurations”
notes.evidence: An alert may display different statuses from different configurations. To update the alert statuses, re-run each out-of-date configuration. Alternatively, you can delete stale configurations from a branch to remove outdated alerts.

notes.front: Where do you delete an unwanted code scanning configuration for one branch of an alert?
notes.back: In the “Configurations analyzing” dialog, opened by clicking the branch under Affected branches; click Delete configuration.
notes.explanation: Clicking Cancel undoes an accidental deletion before the changes are applied.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Removing stale configurations and alerts from a branch”
notes.evidence: To delete an unwanted configuration for the desired branch, click Delete configuration. If you delete a configuration by mistake, click Cancel to avoid applying your changes.

notes.front: Which category label does GitHub give a code scanning alert found in code generated by the build process?
notes.back: Generated.
notes.explanation: Category labels mark alerts that are not found in application code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About labels for alerts that are not found in application code”
notes.evidence: * Generated: Code generated by the build process * Test: Test code * Library: Library or third-party code * Documentation: Documentation

notes.front: Which category label does GitHub give a code scanning alert found in test code?
notes.back: Test.
notes.explanation: The label relates to where the alert is, not to what the problem is.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About labels for alerts that are not found in application code”
notes.evidence: * Generated: Code generated by the build process * Test: Test code * Library: Library or third-party code * Documentation: Documentation

notes.front: Which category label does GitHub give a code scanning alert found in library or third-party code?
notes.back: Library.
notes.explanation: Like the other category labels, it marks code that is not application code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About labels for alerts that are not found in application code”
notes.evidence: * Generated: Code generated by the build process * Test: Test code * Library: Library or third-party code * Documentation: Documentation

notes.front: Which category label does GitHub give a code scanning alert found in documentation?
notes.back: Documentation.
notes.explanation: Code scanning assigns these labels from file paths; you cannot categorise files yourself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About labels for alerts that are not found in application code”
notes.evidence: * Generated: Code generated by the build process * Test: Test code * Library: Library or third-party code * Documentation: Documentation Code scanning categorizes files by file path. You cannot manually categorize source files.

notes.front: Which filter keyword limits the code scanning alert list to alerts in application code?
notes.back: `autofilter:true`, the same as the “Only alerts in application code” filter.
notes.explanation: It leaves out the alerts that carry labels marking them as outside application code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assessing code scanning alerts for your repository”, “Restricting results to application code only”
notes.evidence: You can use the "Only alerts in application code" filter or `autofilter:true` keyword and value to restrict results to alerts in application code.

notes.front: When a code scanning alert has a security severity level, which level does code scanning display and use?
notes.back: The security severity, in preference to the severity.
notes.explanation: Only security alerts found using CodeQL carry a security severity, so other alerts show their severity alone.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert severity and security severity levels”
notes.evidence: Each security alert found using CodeQL also has a security severity level of `Critical`, `High`, `Medium`, or `Low`. When an alert has a security severity level, code scanning displays and uses this level in preference to the `severity`.

notes.front: Which scoring system do code scanning security severity levels follow?
notes.back: The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, which is also used for advisories in the GitHub Advisory Database.
notes.explanation: It is an industry-standard system, not one invented for code scanning.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert severity and security severity levels”
notes.evidence: Security severity levels follow the industry-standard Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) that is also used for advisories in the GitHub Advisory Database.

notes.front: How is the security severity of a new CodeQL security query calculated?
notes.back: As the 75th percentile of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System scores of the CVEs that share the query’s Common Weakness Enumeration tags.
notes.explanation: That one score becomes the query’s security severity, so every alert from the query shares it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “Calculation of security severity levels”
notes.evidence: 1. Search for all CVEs that are assigned one or more of the CWE tags associated with the new security query. 2. Calculate the 75th percentile of the CVSS score for those CVEs. 3. Define that score as the security severity for the query.

notes.front: In which two set-ups do code scanning alerts appear on pull requests as check results and annotations?
notes.back: When code scanning runs as a pull request check, or scans each push and maps results to open pull requests.
notes.explanation: By default, the pull request check covers only pull requests that target the default branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts in pull requests”
notes.evidence: This happens in repositories where code scanning either: * Is configured as a pull request check (by default, this is limited to pull requests that target the default branch) * Is configured to scan each time code is pushed (the results are mapped to any open pull requests)

notes.front: When does a pull request show a code scanning alert?
notes.back: Only when all the lines of code the alert identifies exist in the pull request diff.
notes.explanation: Having only some of an alert’s lines in the diff is not enough.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts in pull requests”
notes.evidence: You will only see an alert in a pull request if all the lines of code identified by the alert exist in the pull request diff.

notes.front: How are code scanning alerts inside a pull request’s diff shown on the Conversation tab?
notes.back: As annotations, in a pull request review that code scanning posts, on the lines that triggered them.
notes.explanation: From an annotation you can comment on the alert, dismiss it or view its paths.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Viewing an alert on your pull request”
notes.evidence: Code scanning posts a pull request review that shows each alert as an annotation on the lines of code that triggered the alert. You can comment on the alerts, dismiss the alerts, and view paths for the alerts, directly from the annotations.

notes.front: Depending on branch protection rules, the “Code scanning results” check may be a {{c1::required check}} that stops a pull request merging until it passes.
notes.explanation: Whether the check blocks merging is decided by the branch protection rules, not by code scanning itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts in pull requests”
notes.evidence: Depending on branch protection rules, the "Code scanning results" check may be a required check that prevents pull requests from being merged until it passes.

notes.front: By default, which severities make the Code scanning results check on a pull request fail?
notes.back: `error`, `critical` or `high`.
notes.explanation: `error` is a severity level; `critical` and `high` are security severity levels.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Managing severity levels for check failures”
notes.evidence: If the code scanning results check finds any problems with a severity of `error`, `critical`, or `high`, the check fails and the error is reported in the check results.

notes.front: Can you change which severities make the code scanning pull request check fail?
notes.back: Yes: in the repository settings you can set the severities and security severities that cause a check failure.
notes.explanation: Without an override, results with a severity of `error`, `critical` or `high` fail the check.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Managing severity levels for check failures”
notes.evidence: You can override the default behavior in your repository settings, by specifying the level of severities and security severities that will cause a pull request check failure.

notes.front: On a pull request, what happens when you push a commit that fixes a code scanning problem?
notes.back: The pull request checks run again; the alert is closed and its annotation removed.
notes.explanation: Anyone with push access to the pull request can make such a fix.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Fixing an alert on your pull request”
notes.evidence: Anyone with push access to a pull request can fix a code scanning alert that's identified on that pull request. If you commit changes to the pull request this triggers a new run of the pull request checks. If your changes fix the problem, the alert is closed and the annotation removed.

notes.front: When might you dismiss a code scanning alert rather than fix it?
notes.back: An error in code used only for testing, or when fixing costs more than the improvement is worth.
notes.explanation: Dismissing is a way of closing an alert that you don’t think needs to be fixed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: Dismissing an alert is a way of closing an alert that you don't think needs to be fixed. For example, an error in code that's used only for testing, or when the effort of fixing the error is greater than the potential benefit of improving the code.

notes.front: How do you dismiss many code scanning alerts for the same reason at once?
notes.back: Filter the summary of alerts, then dismiss all the matching alerts together.
notes.explanation: For instance, you might filter to the alerts tagged with one Common Weakness Enumeration weakness.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing multiple alerts at once”
notes.evidence: If a project has multiple alerts that you want to dismiss for the same reason, you can bulk dismiss them from the summary of alerts. Typically, you'll want to filter the list and then dismiss all of the matching alerts.

notes.front: Why does choosing the right reason matter when you dismiss a code scanning alert?
notes.back: The reason may affect whether the query continues to be included in future analysis.
notes.explanation: This is why the docs advise exploring an alert before dismissing it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: It's important to choose the appropriate reason from the drop-down menu as this may affect whether a query continues to be included in future analysis.

notes.front: Which dismissal reason fits a CodeQL alert raised because the code uses a sanitisation library that CodeQL does not support?
notes.back: `false positive`.
notes.explanation: GitHub suggests also contributing to the CodeQL repository to improve the analysis.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: If you dismiss a CodeQL alert as a false positive result, for example because the code uses a sanitization library that isn't supported, consider contributing to the CodeQL repository and improving the analysis.

notes.front: Which code scanning dismissal reason covers an alert in code that exists only for testing?
notes.back: `used in tests`.
notes.explanation: It is one of the four values the API accepts for `dismissed_reason`.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for code scanning”, “Update a code scanning alert”
notes.evidence: Required when the state is dismissed. The reason for dismissing or closing the alert. Can be one of: `false positive`, `won't fix`, `used in tests`, `mitigated`, `null`

notes.front: Besides `false positive` and `used in tests`, which two dismissal reasons can a code scanning alert have?
notes.back: `won't fix` and `mitigated`.
notes.explanation: A `dismissed_reason` is required whenever an alert’s state is set to dismissed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “REST API endpoints for code scanning”, “Update a code scanning alert”
notes.evidence: Required when the state is dismissed. The reason for dismissing or closing the alert. Can be one of: `false positive`, `won't fix`, `used in tests`, `mitigated`, `null`

notes.front: When you dismiss a code scanning alert, in which branches is it dismissed?
notes.back: In all branches.
notes.explanation: The alert also stops counting towards the project’s current alerts.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: When you dismiss an alert: * It's dismissed in all branches. * The alert is removed from the number of current alerts for your project.

notes.front: Where does a dismissed code scanning alert go, and what is recorded?
notes.back: To the “Closed” list in the summary of alerts, from where it can be reopened; the reason for closing it is recorded.
notes.explanation: You can also add an optional comment giving the context of the dismissal.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: * The alert is moved to the "Closed" list in the summary of alerts, from where you can reopen it, if required. * The reason why you closed the alert is recorded. * Optionally, you can comment on a dismissal to record the context of an alert dismissal.

notes.front: After a code scanning alert is dismissed, what happens the next time code scanning runs on the same code?
notes.back: The same code won’t generate an alert.
notes.explanation: To act on the problem again, you reopen the alert from the Closed list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: * Optionally, you can comment on a dismissal to record the context of an alert dismissal. * Next time code scanning runs, the same code won't generate an alert.

notes.front: You dismissed a code scanning alert but now need to fix it. What do you do?
notes.back: Find it in the list of closed alerts, reopen it, then fix the code.
notes.explanation: A reopened alert is fixed in the same way as any other alert.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Re-opening dismissed alerts”
notes.evidence: If you dismiss an alert but later realize that you need to fix the alert, you can re-open it and fix the problem with the code. Display the list of closed alerts, find the alert, display it, and reopen it. You can then fix the alert in the same way as any other alert.

notes.front: In the code scanning alert list, how do several filters combine?
notes.back: An alert must match all of them, except the `ref`, `branch` and `pr` filters, which show alerts from any of the listed refs.
notes.explanation: So a second `branch:` filter widens the list instead of narrowing it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assessing code scanning alerts for your repository”, “Filtering code scanning alerts”
notes.evidence: If you enter multiple filters, the view will show alerts matching all these filters. For example, `is:closed severity:high branch:main` will only display closed high-severity alerts that are present on the `main` branch. The exception is filters relating to refs (`ref`, `branch` and `pr`)

notes.front: Do you need a GitHub Copilot subscription to use Copilot Autofix?
notes.back: No, and Copilot Autofix does not consume AI credits.
notes.explanation: What matters is the repository: public, or private or internal with a GitHub Code Security licence.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Getting a suggested fix with Copilot Autofix”
notes.evidence: You do not need a subscription to GitHub Copilot to use GitHub Copilot Autofix, and it does not consume AI credits. Copilot Autofix is available to all public repositories on GitHub.com, as well as internal or private repositories owned by organizations and enterprises that have a license for GitHub Code Security.

notes.front: What must you do to enable Copilot Autofix for a repository that uses CodeQL?
notes.back: Nothing extra: enabling code scanning with CodeQL, in default or advanced setup, is enough.
notes.explanation: Copilot Autofix is allowed by default, so it is on unless an administrator has disabled it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Getting a suggested fix with Copilot Autofix”
notes.evidence: Copilot Autofix is allowed by default and enabled for every repository that uses CodeQL, regardless of whether it uses default or advanced setup for code scanning. There is no separate step to enable Copilot Autofix: enabling code scanning with CodeQL is sufficient.

notes.front: Who can disable Copilot Autofix?
notes.back: Administrators at the enterprise, organisation and repository levels.
notes.explanation: Re-enabling it follows the same steps, choosing the option to allow Copilot Autofix.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Getting a suggested fix with Copilot Autofix”
notes.evidence: Administrators at the enterprise, organization, and repository levels can choose to disable Copilot Autofix. If Copilot Autofix has been disabled at your level, you can re-enable it by following the same steps used to disable it and selecting the option to allow Copilot Autofix.

notes.front: Copilot Autofix generates {{c1::a single suggested fix}} for an alert, which you review and apply yourself.
notes.explanation: Nothing changes in the code until a person applies the suggestion.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Getting a suggested fix with Copilot Autofix”
notes.evidence: Copilot Autofix generates a single suggested fix for an alert, which you review and apply yourself.

notes.front: Copilot Autofix works on a {{c1::best-effort}} basis and cannot generate a fix for every alert in every situation.
notes.explanation: It is not guaranteed to succeed every time, so a missing suggestion is expected behaviour.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Generating a suggested fix”
notes.evidence: Copilot Autofix for code scanning alerts won't be able to generate a fix for every alert in every situation. The feature operates on a best-effort basis and is not guaranteed to succeed 100% of the time.

notes.front: On an alert page, what does Create PR with fix do once Copilot Autofix has generated a suggestion?
notes.back: Creates a branch from the default branch, commits the fix and opens a draft pull request.
notes.explanation: You can then test and edit the suggested fix as you would any other fix.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Generating a suggested fix”
notes.evidence: A new branch is created from the default branch, the generated fix is committed and a draft pull request is created. You can test and edit the suggested fix as you would with any other fix.

notes.front: Copilot Autofix supports only a subset of CodeQL queries. What do you see on a pull request alert from an unsupported query?
notes.back: A note telling you that the query is not supported.
notes.explanation: If a supported query’s suggestion fails to generate, the note suggests pushing another commit or contacting support.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Generating Copilot Autofix suggestions and publishing to a pull request”
notes.evidence: On alerts generated from queries that are not supported by Copilot Autofix, you will see a note telling you that the query is not supported. If a suggestion for a supported query fails to generate, you will see a note on the alert prompting you to try pushing another commit or to contact support.

notes.front: With Copilot Autofix enabled, what happens to code scanning alerts found in a pull request?
notes.back: Their details go automatically to a large language model, and any suggested fixes are published as comments on the relevant alerts.
notes.explanation: The alerts still appear in the pull request as normal; the suggestions follow when the analysis is complete.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Generating Copilot Autofix suggestions and publishing to a pull request”
notes.evidence: When Copilot Autofix is enabled for a repository, alerts are displayed in pull requests as normal and information from any alerts found by code scanning is automatically sent to the LLM for processing. When LLM analysis is complete, any results are published as comments on relevant alerts.

notes.front: What must you check before committing a Copilot Autofix suggestion?
notes.back: That it is a good solution for your codebase and keeps the intended behaviour.
notes.explanation: A suggestion only demonstrates a potential solution for the alert.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Assessing and committing an Copilot Autofix suggestion”
notes.evidence: Each Copilot Autofix suggestion demonstrates a potential solution for a code scanning alert in your codebase. You must assess the suggested changes to determine whether they are a good solution for your codebase and to ensure that they maintain the intended behavior.

notes.front: What must be available in a repository for agentic autofix, and what happens without Copilot cloud agent?
notes.back: Copilot cloud agent and Copilot Autofix; without the agent, assigning an alert falls back to Copilot Autofix.
notes.explanation: Agentic autofix is in public preview, so this may change.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Agentic autofix”
notes.evidence: Agentic autofix requires Copilot cloud agent and Copilot Autofix to be available in the repository. If Copilot cloud agent isn't available, assigning an alert falls back to Copilot Autofix instead.

notes.front: How is an agentic autofix session billed?
notes.back: As a Copilot cloud agent session, which consumes AI credits.
notes.explanation: Copilot Autofix, by contrast, does not consume AI credits.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Agentic autofix”
notes.evidence: Each agentic autofix session is billed as a Copilot cloud agent session and consumes AI credits.

notes.front: Why can’t agentic autofix confirm that a fix resolves an alert from the `security-extended` query suite?
notes.back: It validates fixes by re-running CodeQL with the code-scanning query suite only.
notes.explanation: The same applies to custom queries, and fix quality for third-party tools’ alerts is not guaranteed either.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “Agentic autofix”
notes.evidence: Agentic autofix works on a best-effort basis. Copilot validates fixes by re-running CodeQL using the code-scanning query suite, so it can't confirm that a fix resolves alerts generated by custom queries or the security-extended query suite. Fix quality for alerts from third-party tools is also not guaranteed.

notes.front: How many code scanning alerts can you assign to Copilot in one go from the alerts backlog, and what do you get?
notes.back: Between 1 and 25; Copilot works to resolve them in a single pull request.
notes.explanation: The same bulk assignment is possible from a security campaign.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Fixing alerts with Copilot”
notes.evidence: From the code scanning alerts backlog or from a security campaign, select between 1 and 25 alerts and assign them to Copilot, which works to resolve the selected alerts in a single pull request.

notes.front: What does Copilot deliver after you assign it a code scanning alert?
notes.back: Typically within minutes, a draft pull request authored by Copilot, summarising the fix and the validation steps taken.
notes.explanation: To ask for changes, you comment on the pull request and mention Copilot.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Fixing alerts with Copilot”
notes.evidence: Typically within a few minutes, Copilot opens a draft pull request authored by Copilot, with a summary of the fix and the validation steps taken. Review the agent session log for details, and comment on the pull request, mentioning Copilot, to ask it to iterate.

notes.front: Which code scanning merge protection condition concerns alerts that a required tool has found?
notes.back: A required tool finds a code scanning alert of a severity that is defined in the ruleset.
notes.explanation: Any one of the three conditions is enough to block the merge.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Rulesets for code scanning merge protection”
notes.evidence: prevent pull requests from being merged when any of the following conditions are met: * A required tool finds a code scanning alert of a severity that is defined in the ruleset. * A required tool's analysis is still in progress. * A required tool is not configured for the repository.

notes.front: Which code scanning merge protection condition blocks a merge while a scan has not finished?
notes.back: A required tool’s analysis is still in progress.
notes.explanation: Merging waits until the required analysis has finished.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Rulesets for code scanning merge protection”
notes.evidence: prevent pull requests from being merged when any of the following conditions are met: * A required tool finds a code scanning alert of a severity that is defined in the ruleset. * A required tool's analysis is still in progress. * A required tool is not configured for the repository.

notes.front: Which code scanning merge protection condition blocks a merge when a required scanner has never been set up?
notes.back: A required tool is not configured for the repository.
notes.explanation: A missing tool blocks merging just as a finding would.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Rulesets for code scanning merge protection”
notes.evidence: prevent pull requests from being merged when any of the following conditions are met: * A required tool finds a code scanning alert of a severity that is defined in the ruleset. * A required tool's analysis is still in progress. * A required tool is not configured for the repository.

notes.front: On what kind of branch does GitHub say you should typically use code scanning merge protection?
notes.back: Long-lived feature branches, where code must have been analysed before pull requests can merge.
notes.explanation: The point is the guarantee that analysis has happened before a merge.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Rulesets for code scanning merge protection”
notes.evidence: Typically, you should use code scanning merge protection on long-lived feature branches, where you want to guarantee code has been analyzed before pull requests can be merged.

notes.front: Does adding a code scanning rule to a ruleset turn on code scanning?
notes.back: No: you must enable code scanning separately.
notes.explanation: Until you do, the required tool is not configured, which is itself a blocking condition.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Rulesets for code scanning merge protection”
notes.evidence: Configuring a code scanning rule will not automatically enable code scanning.

notes.front: At which levels can you set code scanning merge protection?
notes.back: At the repository level, and at the organisation level on GitHub Enterprise plans only.
notes.explanation: This is what the merge protection page says; the general rulesets page is less clear, as one sentence offers organisation-wide rulesets on GitHub Team too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Availability”
notes.evidence: You can set code scanning merge protection with rulesets: * At the repository level * At the organization level (GitHub Enterprise plans only)

notes.front: Which two kinds of pull request does code scanning merge protection not apply to?
notes.back: Merge queue groups, and Dependabot pull requests analysed by default setup.
notes.explanation: It also requires all the lines an alert identifies to be in the pull request diff.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Exceptions and limitations”
notes.evidence: Merge protection with rulesets will not apply to: * Merge queue groups * Dependabot pull requests analyzed by default setup Additionally, all the lines of code identified by an alert must exist in the pull request diff.

notes.front: An alert is open on `release-2` but has already been fixed on `main`, the default branch. What status does the alert page show at the top?
notes.back: B) Fixed, the status on the default branch
notes.choices:
A) Open, the status on the branch you were looking at
B) Fixed, the status on the default branch
C) Both statuses side by side in the header
D) “In branch”, coloured grey
notes.choicesExplained: A: the page does not report the non-default branch’s status. C: other branches’ statuses appear in the Affected branches section, not in the header. D: grey “in branch” appears only when the alert doesn’t exist on the default branch.
notes.explanation: The alert page reports the default branch even when that conflicts with another branch; `release-2` has its own entry under Affected branches.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assessing code scanning alerts for your repository”, “Filtering code scanning alerts”
notes.evidence: Please note that if you have filtered for alerts on a non-default branch, but the same alerts exist on the default branch, the alert page for any given alert will still only reflect the alert's status on the default branch, even if that status conflicts with the status on a non-default branch.

notes.front: A release manager must know whether an alert is still open on the `hotfix` branch, which is not the default branch. Where should they look?
notes.back: D) The Affected branches section of the alert page
notes.choices:
A) The status at the top of the alert page
B) The Development section of the alert page
C) The tool status page
D) The Affected branches section of the alert page
notes.choicesExplained: A: the main status reflects only the default branch. B: Development lists linked branches and pull requests that will fix the alert, not each branch’s status. C: the tool status page reports on scanning tools, not on one alert.
notes.explanation: Affected branches is where the alert page shows status on non-default branches.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: You can see the status of the alert on non-default branches in the Affected branches section on the right-hand side of the alert page.

notes.front: Four request handlers each pass a query-string value to the same unsafe database call, and CodeQL detects it. What appears in the alert list?
notes.back: D) One alert, with a dropdown of its paths
notes.choices:
A) Four alerts, one per handler
B) Four alerts that link to each other
C) No alert until one handler is changed
D) One alert, with a dropdown of its paths
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: related paths to one vulnerability are grouped, not split into separate alerts. C: nothing in the docs delays the alert.
notes.explanation: Grouping shows the full scope of one vulnerability in one place, and each route can be reviewed from the dropdown.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert details”
notes.evidence: Code scanning groups these related paths under a single alert rather than creating separate alerts for each path, so you can see the full scope of the vulnerability in one place.

notes.front: Reviewing a CodeQL annotation on a pull request, you suspect the analysis missed a sanitisation step before the data reaches the risky call. What should you open?
notes.back: A) Show paths, to see the full route from source to sink
notes.choices:
A) Show paths, to see the full route from source to sink
B) The Code scanning results check summary
C) The Files changed tab
D) The repository’s tool status page
notes.choicesExplained: B: the check summary lists results, not the route the data takes. C: Files changed shows annotations in the diff, not the data flow. D: the tool status page reports on tools, not on one alert’s data flow.
notes.explanation: The path view lets you check whether the data is really untrusted or a sanitisation step between source and sink was missed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Viewing an alert on your pull request”
notes.evidence: In this case you can also view the full path from the source to the code that uses the data (the sink) by clicking **Show paths**. This makes it easy to check whether the data is untrusted or if the analysis failed to recognize a data sanitization step between the source and the sink.

notes.front: A repository runs a CodeQL advanced setup workflow on every push and also uploads CodeQL CLI results from an external server once a quarter. One alert shows fixed from the workflow but open from the external upload. What brings it up to date?
notes.back: A) Re-run the out-of-date configuration, or delete it from the branch if it is stale
notes.choices:
A) Re-run the out-of-date configuration, or delete it from the branch if it is stale
B) Dismiss the alert as `won't fix`
C) Wait: the statuses merge at the next default-branch scan
D) Disable Copilot Autofix
notes.choicesExplained: B: dismissing closes the alert rather than updating a stale status. C: the docs say to re-run each out-of-date configuration, not to wait. D: Autofix plays no part in configuration statuses.
notes.explanation: Each configuration is a separate analysis origin that keeps its own status for the alert.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts from multiple configurations”
notes.evidence: An alert may display different statuses from different configurations. To update the alert statuses, re-run each out-of-date configuration. Alternatively, you can delete stale configurations from a branch to remove outdated alerts.

notes.front: A security lead wants the code scanning list to leave out alerts in test code, build-generated code and vendored libraries. Which filter does that?

notes.choices:
A) `is:open`
B) `branch:main`
C) `autofilter:true`
D) `severity:high`
notes.choicesExplained: A: shows open alerts wherever they are. B: limits the list to one branch, not to application code. D: filters by severity, not by where the code is.
notes.explanation: Test, generated, library and documentation code carry labels marking them as outside application code.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Assessing code scanning alerts for your repository”, “Restricting results to application code only”
notes.evidence: You can use the "Only alerts in application code" filter or `autofilter:true` keyword and value to restrict results to alerts in application code.

notes.front: A colleague says a CodeQL query’s security severity equals the worst score among the CVEs linked to its weakness types. What is the accurate statement?
notes.back: D) It is the 75th percentile of those CVEs’ scores
notes.choices:
A) Correct: the highest score is used
B) It is the average score of those CVEs
C) Each repository’s administrators set it
D) It is the 75th percentile of those CVEs’ scores
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the calculation uses neither the maximum nor the mean. C: the CodeQL engineering team calculates it, not repository administrators.
notes.explanation: The percentile score is then shown on alerts as Critical, High, Medium or Low.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “Calculation of security severity levels”
notes.evidence: Calculate the 75th percentile of the CVSS score for those CVEs. 3. Define that score as the security severity for the query.

notes.front: An alert’s path identifies lines in two files. A pull request changes one of those files and leaves the other untouched. Does the pull request show the alert?
notes.back: B) No: all of the alert’s lines must be in the diff
notes.choices:
A) Yes: any overlap with the diff is enough
B) No: all of the alert’s lines must be in the diff
C) Yes, but only on the Files changed tab
D) Only if the pull request targets the default branch

notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alerts in pull requests”
notes.evidence: You will only see an alert in a pull request if all the lines of code identified by the alert exist in the pull request diff.

notes.front: A pull request’s code scanning results hold one `Warning` alert and one alert with security severity `Medium`. Default settings apply. What happens to the Code scanning results check?
notes.back: A) It succeeds, with the alerts treated as warnings or notes
notes.choices:
A) It succeeds, with the alerts treated as warnings or notes
B) It fails because of the `Medium` alert
C) It fails because of the `Warning` alert
D) It stays pending until both alerts are dismissed
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: by default only `error`, `critical` or `high` results fail the check. D: the check completes; nobody needs to dismiss anything.
notes.explanation: Both results are below the default failing levels.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Triaging code scanning alerts in pull requests”, “Managing severity levels for check failures”
notes.evidence: If the code scanning results check finds any problems with a severity of `error`, `critical`, or `high`, the check fails and the error is reported in the check results. If all the results found by code scanning have lower severities, the alerts are treated as warnings or notes and the check succeeds.

notes.front: A contractor has read permission on a repository. What code scanning information can they see?
notes.back: B) Code scanning annotations on pull requests, but not the full alert summary
notes.choices:
A) Everything, including the alert summary on the Security and quality tab
B) Code scanning annotations on pull requests, but not the full alert summary

Viewing the alerts for a repository You need write permission to view a summary of all the alerts for a repository on the shield Security and quality tab.

notes.front: A developer merges a change to the default branch that removes the vulnerable code behind an open code scanning alert. What must they do to close the alert?

notes.front: An alert exists on both `main`, the default branch, and `develop`. A maintainer dismisses it from the alert page. What is its state on `develop`?

A) Still open until it is dismissed there too
B) Deleted from the branch
C) Fixed

notes.evidence: There are two ways to get a fix for an alert: agentic autofix and Copilot Autofix. If Copilot cloud agent is available in a repository, assigning an alert uses agentic autofix instead of Copilot Autofix.

notes.front: Is `Warning` a severity level or a security severity level?
notes.back: A severity level, alongside `Error` and `Note`.

notes.evidence: All code scanning alerts have a level of `Error`, `Warning`, or `Note`. * Security severity. Each security alert found using CodeQL also has a security severity level of `Critical`, `High`, `Medium`, or `Low`.

notes.front: Is `High` a severity level or a security severity level?
notes.back: A security severity level.

notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert severity and security severity levels”
notes.evidence: Each security alert found using CodeQL also has a security severity level of `Critical`, `High`, `Medium`, or `Low`. When an alert has a security severity level, code scanning displays and uses this level in preference to the `severity`.

notes.front: How do severity and security severity differ on code scanning alerts?
notes.back: Every alert has a severity; only CodeQL security alerts add a security severity, which takes precedence when present.
notes.explanation: A CodeQL security alert is therefore shown by its security severity, while other alerts show their severity.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning alerts”, “About alert severity and security severity levels”
notes.evidence: All code scanning alerts have a level of `Error`, `Warning`, or `Note`. * Security severity. Each security alert found using CodeQL also has a security severity level of `Critical`, `High`, `Medium`, or `Low`. When an alert has a security severity level, code scanning displays and uses this level in preference to the `severity`.

notes.front: What is the difference between fixing and dismissing a code scanning alert?
notes.back: Fixing changes the code so the problem is gone; dismissing closes the alert without a code change, for alerts you don’t think need fixing.
notes.explanation: Both close the alert, and a dismissed alert can later be reopened from the Closed list.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Resolving code scanning alerts”, “Dismissing alerts”
notes.evidence: There are two ways of closing an alert. You can fix the problem in the code, or you can dismiss the alert. Dismissing an alert is a way of closing an alert that you don't think needs to be fixed.

notes.front: How does Copilot Autofix differ from agentic autofix?
notes.back: Copilot Autofix gives one suggestion you apply yourself; agentic autofix runs a Copilot cloud agent session that validates a fix and opens a pull request.
notes.explanation: Which one you get when assigning an alert depends on whether Copilot cloud agent is available in the repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About autofix for code scanning”, “How autofix works”
notes.evidence: There are two ways to get a fix for an alert: agentic autofix and Copilot Autofix. If Copilot cloud agent is available in a repository, assigning an alert uses agentic autofix instead of Copilot Autofix.

notes.front: How does code scanning merge protection relate to status checks such as Code scanning results?
notes.back: It is not related to them: it blocks merging through ruleset rules, separately from any required status check.
notes.explanation: The Code scanning results check blocks merging only where branch protection rules make it a required check.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Code scanning merge protection”, “Rulesets for code scanning merge protection”
notes.evidence: Merge protection with rulesets is not related to status checks.
